title: Afternoon ambush: reading storm towers
teaches: Will today’s puffy clouds blow up into a thunderstorm, and when should you get indoors? Latent heat and towering heaps, castle turrets at breakfast, the anvil, the gust front, counting the thunder and the 30-30 rule

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Inside a cloud, condensing water gives off heat, so cloudy air cools only about 5 °C per kilometre (about 3 °F per 1,000 feet), not 10. That is why a heap, once it forms, can keep climbing.

Watch the heaps grow: flat **humilis** is fair weather, **mediocris** as tall as wide, towering **congestus** by midday is the warning. Little castle turrets on morning altocumulus (**castellanus**) say the middle sky is already unstable.
A tower that reaches the **tropopause**, 10 to 12 km up, spreads into an ice anvil: a **cumulonimbus**, or thunderstorm. It lives about an hour.
A sudden rush of cool, gusty wind on a hot afternoon is the storm’s downdraught arriving, the **gust front**, usually 5 to 15 minutes before the downpour and the lightning.
Count from flash to bang: 3 seconds per kilometre (5 per mile). Under 30 seconds, get indoors, and stay in until 30 minutes after the last thunder: the **30-30 rule**.

blocks.text: Lesson 1’s small heaps were fair weather because something stopped them growing. On some summer days nothing does. By lunchtime the puffs have become towers, and by mid-afternoon one of them is throwing lightning across the county. This lesson is about seeing that coming, and knowing when to go in.

Why doesn’t a rising bubble stop once it reaches the cloud base? When water evaporates, it absorbs heat energy, which is why sweat cools your skin as it dries. When water vapour condenses back into liquid droplets inside a cloud, it releases that stored heat back into the surrounding air. Meteorologists call it **latent heat**, from the Latin for hidden. That heat warms the cloudy parcel from within, so above the cloud base the rising air cools by only about 5 °C per kilometre instead of 10 °C.

Whether the parcel keeps rising still depends on comparing its cooling rate with the air around it. Often the surrounding air a kilometre or two up gets colder by 6 or 7 °C per kilometre. A dry thermal cooling at 10 °C per kilometre would quickly become colder than that surrounding air and stop rising. A cloudy thermal cooling at 5 °C per kilometre stays warmer than its surroundings, so its buoyancy increases and it keeps billowing upward in bright, cauliflower-like towers.

So the same sky can be stable for a clear bubble and unstable for a cloudy one. Air that cools 6 or 7 °C per kilometre would stop a dry thermal, but not a cloudy one. And below the cloud base, a thermal is not fighting that air at all: on a sunny afternoon the thermals themselves have stirred the lowest kilometre until it cools at about 10 °C per kilometre, just like the bubbles, so a bubble only a degree warmer than the rest keeps that lead all the way up to its dew point. Below the base the sun does the work; above it, the heat from condensing water does.

blocks.title: The stability test, in full
points: Compare two rates: how fast the **air around** gets colder as you go up, and how fast a **rising bubble** cools.
A clear bubble cools about 10 °C per kilometre. A cloudy one cools only about 5, because condensing water warms it.
If the air around cools faster than the bubble, the bubble stays warmer and keeps rising: **unstable**. If slower, the bubble ends up colder and sinks back: **stable**.
So air that cools 6 or 7 °C per kilometre is stable for a clear bubble but unstable for a cloudy one. That is why a cumulus, once it forms, can keep on growing.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height: the air around, and a bubble before and after it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Three factors control where the rising air stops. First, **sunlight** warming the ground sets the starting temperature of the thermals. Second, low-level **moisture** sets the height of the cloud base, determining how soon the rising parcel switches to the slower 5 °C per kilometre cooling rate. Third, a stable [[inversion|env]] aloft can cap the cloud completely, just as an inversion flattens stratocumulus on the low floor. When a rising cloud top pokes into a warmer layer of air above it, the cloudy parcel immediately becomes colder and denser than its surroundings and cannot climb any higher.

Meteorologists classify cumulus clouds into three species according to their vertical growth. **Cumulus humilis** is small and flattened, wider than it is tall, and signals fair weather. **Cumulus mediocris** grows roughly as tall as it is wide. **Cumulus congestus** builds into tall, billowing cauliflower towers, and it is the stage to watch closely: on a deeply unstable day, a congestus tower can keep growing into a full thunderstorm.

The middle floor can give you an even earlier warning, at breakfast. If you spot miniature turrets sprouting upward from a line of altocumulus on a warm, humid morning, that is altocumulus castellanus, from the Latin for castle-like. Those little towers tell you that the middle sky is cooling with height faster than the 5 °C per kilometre of a rising cloudy parcel, so parcels rising out of the cloud layer stay warmer than their surroundings and keep climbing on their own. On a normal day, the afternoon thermals are capped well below the middle floor; when castellanus appears in the morning, it warns that the middle floor is already unstable and afternoon thermals can punch all the way up into thunderstorms.

Forecasters and glider pilots track this vertical growth on a temperature-height chart called a **sounding**. Twice a day, weather stations release balloons carrying a radio transmitter, thermometer, and humidity sensor that measure the temperature and dew point every few seconds as the balloon ascends.

In the figure below, the solid violet line shows the balloon’s report of the surrounding air temperature at each altitude. (The dashed violet line shows the cooler dawn profile before sunlight warmed the ground.) The teal line shows the dew point, and the orange line traces a rising parcel, cooling at 10 °C per kilometre below the cloud base and about 5 °C per kilometre above it. Read the chart this way: **temperature runs along the bottom**, warmer to the right, and **height runs up the side**. Air that gets colder quickly as you climb leans steeply to the left, so the further the violet line tilts left, the faster the air around cools with height and the more unstable the day. At any altitude where the orange parcel line lies to the right of the violet environment line, the parcel is warmer than the surrounding air and keeps accelerating upward. Where the two lines cross, the parcel loses its buoyancy and stops.

blocks.caption: A summer day over farm country, with a warm layer a couple of kilometres up.
blocks.task: Grow a cumulus congestus: a tower several kilometres tall.

blocks.text: If there is no low-level inversion to cap a growing tower, it can climb to an altitude of 10 to 12 kilometres. Throughout the lowest layer of the atmosphere (the troposphere), the air generally gets colder with height because it is heated from below by the sun-warmed ground. Around 10 to 12 kilometres up, however, the temperature stops falling with altitude and begins to rise instead.

This upper warming is caused by **ozone**, a three-atom form of oxygen (O₃). High in the atmosphere, intense ultraviolet light from the sun splits ordinary two-atom oxygen molecules (O₂) apart, and the free oxygen atoms combine with intact oxygen molecules to form an ozone layer. Ozone strongly absorbs incoming ultraviolet radiation, heating the upper atmosphere from above while shielding the surface below.

The boundary where temperature stops falling and starts rising with height is the **tropopause**, marking the base of the **stratosphere**. Because the stratosphere gets warmer with altitude, it acts as a massive, permanent inversion lid across the top of the troposphere that even the strongest thunderstorm updraughts cannot penetrate far.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height, from the ground into the stratosphere.

blocks.text: When a rising storm tower slams into the stable tropopause, the buoyant air continuing to surge up from below cannot climb much higher and spreads out horizontally instead, like a fountain jet hitting a ceiling. At that altitude the cloud water is completely frozen, so the spreading ice crystals fan out into a broad, flat **anvil** with fibrous edges. Strong upper-level winds blow the anvil far downwind, usually stretching it out ahead of the storm’s path. Once a towering heap develops an icy upper region and begins dropping rain from its base, it has become a **cumulonimbus**, or thunderstorm.

In the next figure, you can also adjust how rapidly the surrounding atmosphere cools with height. Because a rising parcel inside the cloud cools at roughly 5 °C per kilometre, a faster cooling rate in the surrounding air (the violet line tilting further left) gives the cloudy parcel a larger temperature lead and stronger upward acceleration.

blocks.caption: The same day, with the instability control added.
blocks.task: Remove the lid and make the air unstable enough to grow a cumulonimbus.

blocks.text: An individual thunderstorm cell goes through a three-stage life cycle that lasts about an hour.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell, from first heap to last shower.
blocks.task: Run the storm to the end of its life.

blocks.text: In the **growing stage** (or cumulus stage), the tower consists entirely of warm updraughts carrying moist air skyward and building the cloud upward.

The **mature stage** begins when precipitation inside the cloud grows too heavy for the updraughts to support and starts falling toward the ground. Inside strong, gusty updraughts, ice pellets are repeatedly carried up and tumbled through dense clouds of supercooled droplets that freeze onto them in concentric layers, building **hailstones** until they are heavy enough to fall out of the storm.

As heavy rain and hail plunge downward, they drag surrounding air down with them. At the same time, drier air mixes into the edges of the storm and evaporates some of the falling rain, chilling the air and making it denser so it plunges faster still. During this mature stage, the storm contains a warm updraught and a cold downdraught side by side, producing its heaviest downpours, hail, lightning, and sudden surface wind gusts.

Finally, in the **dissipating stage**, the cold downdraught spreads out across the ground like a miniature cold front, cutting off the inflow of warm, humid air that fuelled the updraught. Starved of warm air from below, the storm rains itself out, often leaving its orphaned ice anvil lingering high overhead.

That downdraught gives you a warning you can feel. On a hot, still afternoon, a sudden rush of cool, gusty wind, often raising a wall of dust off the fields, is the cold air from the storm’s downdraught spreading out along the ground ahead of it: the **gust front**. It usually arrives 5 to 15 minutes before the downpour and the lightning. When the air turns suddenly cool and blustery under a dark tower, that is the time to get in, not when the first drops fall.

Inside a churning cumulonimbus tower, soft hailstones (graupel), ice crystals, and supercooled droplets constantly collide with one another. All atoms have negatively charged **electrons** on their outer shells, and when two objects rub or collide, electric charge can transfer from one surface to the other, just as rubbing a balloon on your hair leaves one negatively charged and the other positively charged.

In the mixed-phase zone of a thunderstorm, collisions between small ice crystals and heavier pellets of soft hail systematically leave the tiny ice crystals with a slight positive charge and the heavier hail pellets with a negative charge. The storm’s updraught sweeps the lightweight, positively charged ice crystals high into the anvil while gravity pulls the heavier, negatively charged hail into the middle and lower parts of the cloud, separating electrical charge on a massive scale.

blocks.caption: Where a thunderstorm keeps its charge.

blocks.text: Once the voltage difference between these regions (or between the cloud base and the ground) grows strong enough, the electric field strips electrons directly off air molecules, ionizing the air into an electrically conducting plasma channel. Stored charge surges through that narrow channel in a violent spark several kilometres long: **lightning**.

A lightning stroke heats the narrow channel of air to roughly 30,000 °C in a few millionths of a second—about five times hotter than the surface of the sun. Superheated that rapidly, the air has no time to expand gently; it explodes outward at supersonic speed, creating a shock wave that decays into the booming sound wave we hear as **thunder**.

Because light travels at 300,000 kilometres per second, you see the lightning flash the instant it happens. Sound travels through air much more slowly, at about **343 metres per second**, taking roughly **three seconds to travel one kilometre**, or about five seconds a mile. By counting the seconds between the flash and the first crack of thunder and dividing by three, you can find how many kilometres away the lightning struck. (The figure speeds up the clock so you don’t have to wait in real time, while displaying the actual number of seconds you would count.)

blocks.caption: A storm somewhere off over the hills.
blocks.task: Make the storm strike, and count.

blocks.text: Lightning does not only strike directly beneath the dark rain core. Because strong positive charge accumulates high up in the spreading anvil, a powerful lightning bolt can arc outward from the upper cloud through clear air and strike the ground ten kilometres or more away from the rain shaft, a hazard known as a "bolt from the blue."

The safety rule follows from this, and it is easy to remember as the **30-30 rule**: if you count fewer than thirty seconds between flash and thunder, the storm is within ten kilometres and close enough to strike you. Get indoors straight away, away from open ground and ridges, and stay under cover until thirty minutes after the last rumble of thunder. A dying anvil can still fire a late bolt when the rain seems to be over.

Beneath the spreading anvil of a mature thunderstorm, the underside of the cloud sometimes develops smooth, rounded pouches hanging toward the ground. The anvil contains a heavy load of ice crystals and water droplets. When pockets of this particle-laden air sink into the drier air below the anvil base, the ice and droplets begin to evaporate (or sublimate), absorbing latent heat from the sinking parcel. Because that evaporation cools the air, the sinking parcel warms at only about 5 °C per kilometre as it descends, whereas the clear air surrounding it warms with decreasing altitude by 6 or 7 °C per kilometre. Staying colder and denser than the air around it, the cloudy pocket continues to sink in smooth, rounded lobes—essentially convection running upside down, driven by evaporation inside sinking air just as a cumulus tower is driven upward by condensation inside rising air.

blocks.caption: The underside of an anvil, late in a storm.
blocks.task: Let the cold air sink until pouches form.

blocks.text: These hanging pouches are called **mammatus** (or mamma). Although they look dramatic, especially when lit from the side by low evening sunlight, the pouches themselves are harmless descending air. Because they form underneath the spreading anvil, you will most often see them either well ahead of an approaching storm or trailing behind after the main storm core has passed.

blocks.title: Reading storm towers
points: Castle turrets on the morning altocumulus: the middle sky is unstable. Watch the afternoon.
Heaps already towering into cauliflower congestus by midday on a hot, humid day: storms likely by mid-afternoon.
A strong inversion on the morning sounding, or heaps that spread flat: no storms today.
A sudden cool, gusty wind on a hot afternoon: the gust front. Get in now.
Flash to bang under 30 seconds: indoors. Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

blocks.text: First name each cloud in the photos, then read what a few changing skies are up to.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Cumulus heaps are already towering into congestus by midday on a hot, humid day. What should you expect by mid-afternoon?
options: Thunderstorms, as the towers reach the tropopause
Steady frontal rain, setting in for the whole night
Clearing skies, as the heaps use up their moisture
items.why: Cumulus towers that are already growing tall by midday in a deeply unstable atmosphere often reach the tropopause by afternoon, developing into cumulonimbus thunderstorms with lightning, downpours, and gusty winds.

items.question: The morning balloon sounding shows a strong temperature inversion two kilometres up. What will today’s cumulus heaps do?
options: Grow into thunderstorms, as the warm layer feeds them heat
Flatten out under the lid, and the day stays fair
Sink back down to the ground and turn into valley fog
items.why: When rising cumulus clouds hit a warmer inversion layer aloft, they become colder and denser than their surroundings and cannot climb through the cap.

items.question: You see a flash of lightning and hear thunder 12 seconds later. Roughly how far away was the strike?
items.why: Sound travels about one kilometre every three seconds (a mile every five), so 12 ÷ 3 gives 4 km: well within the 10 km danger zone where everyone should get indoors.

items.question: The rain has stopped and the last rumble of thunder was ten minutes ago. Is it safe to go back outside?
options: Yes: once the rain stops, the storm has passed on
Yes, as long as there is blue sky right overhead
Not yet: wait thirty minutes after the last thunder
items.why: A dissipating storm anvil can still discharge lightning up to ten kilometres away through clear air; wait a full thirty minutes after the last thunder before going back out.

items.question: At dawn, miniature castle-like turrets sprout from a middle-level line of altocumulus. What should you expect?
options: A calm, settled day, as turrets mean the air is drying out
Radiation fog tonight, as the turrets sink after sunset
Thunderstorms this afternoon, as the middle sky is unstable
items.why: Altocumulus castellanus shows that the middle floor is already unstable in the morning, meaning afternoon thermals will have no stable cap to stop them from growing into thunderstorms.

items.question: It’s a hot, still afternoon under a dark tower to the west. Suddenly the air turns cool and a gusty wind kicks up dust. No rain has fallen yet. What is happening?
options: The gust front: the downpour and lightning are minutes away
The storm is dying: its cold air means it has run out of heat
A cold front: a day of steady rain is setting in behind it
items.why: The cool rush is the storm’s downdraught spreading out along the ground ahead of it. It usually leads the downpour and the lightning by 5 to 15 minutes: time to get in.

learned: Condensing water releases latent heat, so cloudy air cools only about 5 °C per kilometre (about 3 °F per 1,000 feet) instead of 10; air that cools 6 or 7 °C per kilometre is stable for a clear bubble but unstable for a cloudy one, which is why a heap can keep growing.
Heaps are classed by growth as humilis, mediocris or congestus; an inversion aloft caps them. Castellanus turrets on morning altocumulus warn that the middle sky is unstable.
On a sounding, temperature runs along the bottom and height up the side, so air that cools faster with height tilts further left.
The tropopause (10 to 12 km up) is a lid warmed by ozone; a tower that reaches it spreads into an ice anvil, a cumulonimbus. A cell grows, matures and dies in about an hour.
A sudden cool, gusty wind on a hot afternoon is the storm’s gust front, 5 to 15 minutes ahead of the downpour and lightning.

Thunder travels about 3 seconds per kilometre (5 per mile). Under 30 seconds, get indoors, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder: the 30-30 rule. Mammatus pouches under an anvil are harmless sinking air.

cumulonimbus.title: Cumulonimbus
cumulonimbus.text: A towering convective cloud that climbs all the way to the tropopause (10 to 12 km up), where its frozen top flattens and spreads into a fibrous anvil. A single cell grows, matures, and dissipates in about an hour, capable of producing heavy downpours, hail, strong downdraught gusts, and lightning.

lightning.title: Counting the thunder
lightning.text: Collisions between soft hail and ice crystals inside a storm separate electric charge until a massive spark discharges as lightning, heating the air channel to about 30,000 °C and generating the shock wave we hear as thunder. Sound travels about one kilometre every three seconds (a mile every five), so dividing the seconds between flash and thunder by three gives the distance in kilometres. The 30-30 rule: if the count is under 30 seconds, get indoors, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

mammatus.title: Mammatus
mammatus.text: Smooth, rounded pouches hanging beneath a thunderstorm anvil, formed where pockets of ice- and droplet-laden air sink into drier air below. Evaporating particles chill the sinking parcels so they remain denser than their surroundings, driving upside-down convection. While they indicate a strong storm nearby, the pouches themselves are harmless.
